summary: At the gate of Nain, Jesus meets a widow burying her only son, has compassion on her, and raises the young man to life with a word.
key_insight: No one asked Jesus for anything. There was no request and no word of faith; Luke says simply that when the Lord saw the widow, He had compassion on her. The miracle begins in His heart.
story: The next day Jesus went to a town called Nain. Many of His disciples went with Him, and a large crowd.
As He came near the town gate, a funeral procession was coming out. The dead man was the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A large crowd from the town walked with her.

When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” Then He came and touched the open coffin, and those who carried it stood still. He said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.”
The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus presented him to his mother.

Fear came on everyone, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has risen up among us”; and, “God has visited His people.” The report about Jesus went out through all Judea and all the surrounding region.

scene.label: Nain
scene.text: A small town on the north slope of the Hill of Moreh, about six miles southeast of Nazareth and roughly twenty-five miles from Capernaum, a long day’s walk. On the far side of the same hill lay Shunem, where Elisha raised a mother’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37).

scene.label: A widow’s only son
scene.text: A widow who lost her only son lost her provider and her protector, and with him the family line. The prophets used mourning for an only son as their picture of the deepest grief (Jeremiah 6:26; Amos 8:10).

scene.label: Burial customs
scene.text: Burial usually took place on the day of death, outside the town. The body, wrapped in cloth, lay on an open bier, and family, neighbors and mourners walked with it. Contact with the dead made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11).

scene.label: Elijah’s echo
scene.text: Elijah raised a widow’s son at Zarephath and “gave him to his mother” (1 Kings 17:23). In Greek, Luke uses the very words of the Greek Old Testament there: Jesus “presented him to his mother.” No wonder the crowd said, “A great prophet has risen up among us.”

witnesses.luke: Luke alone tells this story, one of many widows in his Gospel, from Anna in the temple to the widow with two mites. He places it just before John the Baptist’s messengers arrive, so when Jesus answers them that “the dead are raised” (7:22), the reader has just seen it. Here, for the first time, Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his own narration.

seeing.reveals: Jesus, whom Luke here calls “the Lord,” meets death on the road and overrules it with a word. His power moves at the prompting of His compassion, before anyone asks.
seeing.living: Jesus spoke to the grieving mother before He spoke to the dead son: “Do not weep.” He can say that because He can do something about the grief. Tell Him the sorrow you have stopped expecting Him to notice, and look for the widows and mourners in your own town as He did.
seeing.ponder: What grief are you carrying that you have not believed Jesus sees?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus meets death with compassion and a word, and gives back what was lost.
outline: Two crowds meet at the gate (11–12)
preaching.watch_for: The crowd’s cry, “God has visited His people” (v. 16), picks up Zacharias’ song at the start of the Gospel: “He has visited and redeemed His people” (Luke 1:68). In Jesus, God’s promised visit has come.
